en: [Homage, auspicious invocation, etc.

Here, however, the stage of generation (*utpattikrama*) must be explained. Regarding that, the *Sādhana-sūtra* in thirty-two [verses], which is the purification of the thirty-two marks of a Great Being (*mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*), was spoken by Jālandhari-pāda; and we shall explain that in due order.
The wheel of worship, the fourfold Brahmavihāra, the supreme innate [nature],
one's own chosen deity, the protection wheel, and the resolve upon emptiness.
The charnel ground, the peaked palace, the clearly manifest causal maṇḍala,
swift attainment, the arising, the placement, and the deity’s own body.
Homage to Śrī Heruka!
Having prostrated before that Lord Śrī Heruka, who is the innate one with a white body, possessing two arms and one face, and whose nature consists of both the empty and the non-empty;
The practitioner of mantra should state the sādhana for those forms transformed from that [Nairātmyā], such as the sixteen-armed and so forth, as well as for Nairātmyā herself.

In this regard, there is the commentary titled *Vajrapradīpa* on the *Vicitrahevajrasādhana* composed by the venerable master Saroruhapāda, the work of Śrījālandharipāda. For that very reason, there is the *Dveṣavajrasādhana*, the work of Bhadrapāda, which illuminates those respective meanings. Furthermore, thinking that it cannot be meditated upon by one of dull intellect after merely hearing it, and having extracted [the essentials] from the *Vajrapradīpa* and the *Dveṣavajrasādhana* commentaries on that *Sādhana*, and following the *Mūlatantra*, I shall now combine the *utpattikrama* and *utpannakrama* sādhanas so that they may be properly understood by the mind of one with dull intellect. It is also said in the *Hevajra*:
The teaching of the Dharma by the Vajra-holder relies upon two stages: the stage of generation and indeed the stage of completion.
In this regard, the means of accomplishment for the stage of generation should also be understood by following other sūtras such as the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
Emission, the wheel of gnosis, consecration, as well as sealing,
the tasting of nectar, the activity for the world, the six limbs, and the clear light.
Rising, the recitation of mantras, the offering (bali), the yoga called "subtle" (sūkṣma),
again the ritual placement (nyāsa), the wandering (vihāra), eating, walking, and sleeping, and rising once more— thus is the compendium of the thirty-two aphorisms.
1. The Circle of Worship (pūjācakra)

First, having initially undertaken the instructions on the four bases of training, the taking of the three refuges, and so forth, up to the *poṣadha* vows; having trained well in the six perfections and propitiated a Vajrācārya; and having entered the maṇḍala as described in the *Śrī Hevajra*, receiving the initiations in the proper sequence; the yogin—whose mind is intent upon the welfare of all sentient beings and who desires to accomplish the glorious *Hevajra*—should practice the accomplishment of the glorious *Hevajra* in a secret, secluded place agreeable to his mind, seated upon a comfortable seat marked with a double-vajra in the vajra-paryaṅka posture, until the attainment of "heat" (*ūṣmā*) occurs. Having recited "I am Śrī Heruka" three times, he should focus upon his chosen deity according to the sequence to be described and perform the protection of the place, himself, and the yoga.
Oṃ rakṣa 2 hūṃ 3 phaṭ svāhā || Oṃ vajrasattva hūṃ || Oṃ āḥ hūṃ ||

Thereafter, having visualized within the lotus of one’s own heart a blue syllable *vaṃ* and *hūṃ* upon a sun disc produced from the letter *ra*, emitting five-colored rays of light; and having illuminated infinite world-systems with those rays, one should visualize in the sky before oneself one’s chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) surrounded by the circle of yoginīs such as Gaurī, together with the gurus, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas, and worship them with the special offerings of the outer, secret, and essential (*tattva*) types. In that regard, the outer offering consists of the act of pleasing [the deities] with sixteen goddesses—beginning with Vīṇā and ending with Dharmā—who have emerged from the seed-syllable in one’s own heart, each holding her respective hand-symbol and gesture as will be described. The secret offering is the meditation on the presentation of the substances of the pledge (*samaya*) according to their secret conventions, held in the hands of the goddesses such as Gaurī who reside in that mandala circle. In this context:
Gaurī holds a deer-marked moon; Caurī holds a vessel of the sun;
Vettālī has water in her hand; and Ghasmarī holds medicine.
Pukkasī should hold a club, and Śabarī should be the bearer of nectar;
Caṇḍālī should play the hand-drum, and Ḍombī should display an embrace.

The reality known as the "expanding and contracting form" arises from the experience of the bliss of the meditative absorption on selflessness (*nairātmya*). That itself is the "worship of reality. Having performed that worship before the Blessed One, one should perform the confession of misdeeds and so forth:
"In this beginningless saṃsāra, through the deceptions of the whirlpools of birth, whatever sinful karma has been committed, caused to be committed, or rejoiced in."
I confess all that, indeed so as never to do it again; and I rejoice, according to its true nature, in whatever merit belongs to all living beings.
Likewise, [one should know] the merit of worldly deities, of Buddhas, of those who wander alone like rhinoceroses, of Śrāvaka-Buddhas, and of the Perfectly Awakened Protectors.

Whatever merit is associated with this rejoicing, I dedicate toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment for the sake of generating the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*) in all sentient beings. I go for refuge until I reach the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) to the Blessed One, the sole embodiment of the three realms, the abode of the bliss of innate joy (*sahajānanda*), the glorious hero Heruka, the Buddha; to the Dharma consisting of the maṇḍala, mudrās, mantras, and so forth taught by him; and to the Saṅgha, the assembly of goddesses such as Gaurī and others who abide within that wheel. For the sake of accomplishing the welfare of all sentient beings, I generate the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*), which is the indivisibility of emptiness and compassion, characterized by the emptiness endowed with the excellence of all aspects, directed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—the supreme path.

I take refuge in what is called the Vajrayāna; furthermore, I offer myself to those [beings] for the sake of providing all forms of happiness to all sentient beings. This is the first chapter, titled "The Wheel of Worship. 1.
2. The Four Brahmavihāras

Thereafter, having reflected that all sentient beings—whether they have been my mothers, fathers, brothers, sisters, or others throughout my beginningless cycle of existence—are indeed such beings, one should cultivate great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*) characterized by the affection felt for an only son. Then, seeing them all fallen into the ocean of saṃsāra and without refuge, the practitioner, feeling distressed and lamenting, should meditate on great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), which is by nature the longing to deliver them from suffering or the causes of suffering. Having generated the great resolve, thinking "I must establish all beings in perfect enlightenment," and perceiving oneself as perfected in the form of Śrī Heruka, one laughs; this is sympathetic joy (*muditā*). Thinking, "It is not fitting for me to grasp at gain or loss, praise or blame, fame or insignificance, pleasure or pain, and so forth," one should cultivate the fourth [immeasurable], equanimity (*upekṣā*), characterized by freedom from the eight worldly dharmas. Thus concludes the four sublime abodes (*caturbrahmavihāra*). ||2||

3. Following that, having meditated upon oneself as being overcome by a corpse, and having perceived the non-existence of the ordinary body through the yoga of the *jñānālokavajra-samādhi*, one should meditate—by means of the excellent instruction—on the manifestation of the meaning of the four syllables "Śrī Heruka. By this, there is the non-existence of the impure body; thus, it is "supreme" (*paramam*). ||3||
4. Innate (sahaja)

Thereafter, one should instantly contemplate the arising of Sahajanātha. Instantly, in the center of the Buddha-abode, one should visualize Sahajaheruka, who is described by the syllable *vaṃ*: he is Vajrasattva, the Great Peace; he wears a crown of matted locks, sits in the vajra-paryaṅka posture upon a corpse on a double lotus (*viśvapadma*) with a moon seat; he has two arms and one face, is white in color, possesses three eyes, and his two hands hold the *dharmamudrā*; he bears the thirty-two major marks and is adorned with the eighty minor signs. By this, the following is established: that which is described by the syllable *vaṃ* from the six-syllable mantra "Śrīherukavajra" is the Supreme Vajrasattva known as Sahajaheruka; thus, he is "Sahaja" (the Innate). ||4||

One’s own chosen deity resides in his heart: a sun disk transformed from the letter *jraṃ*; above that, a full moon disk formed by the transformation of its half-moon and bindu; and in the center of that, the syllable *hūṃ*, the seed of the world’s birth, indicated by the letter *ja*. It is black in color and most terrifying. One should meditate on the *vajra* transformed from the syllable *hūṃ*, with the reality (*hūṃ-tattva*) situated in the center of the hub of that *vajra*.

Thereafter, having visualized a mere lunar disc through the transformation of the seed-syllable marked by the signs of the sun and moon, and having seen the most terrifying Dveṣavajrin emerging from that [disc] in the sky, one should cause him to enter [oneself] according to the instruction to be described—by way of the analogy of milk and water—and contemplate the Lord in the form of one's own chosen deity, consisting of the three beings (trisattva).
One should visualize the Lord of the Mandala as arisen from the reflection of the sentient being.
Thus, according to this statement, [one should meditate upon] one's own chosen deity. ||5||

6. Having thus meditated upon the protection wheel, which is extremely terrible with eight faces and so forth, as the Hatred-Vajra, one should emit the ten wrathful deities born from the syllable *HŪṂ*, surrounded by garlands of flames, into the directions beginning with the east. Therein, in the east, is Yamāntaka, crowned with Vairocana, of great black color, holding a vajra-mallet in his hand. In the south is Prajñāntaka, crowned with Ratnasaṃbhava, of great white [color]—

[One should visualize] Sitadaṇḍadhara, who is white in color; in the west, Padmāntaka, crowned with Amitābha, who is deep red in color and holds a red lotus; in the north, Vighnāntaka, crowned with Akṣobhya, who is deep blue in color and holds a formidable vajra; in the northeast, Acala, who is deep black and holds a sword; in the southeast, Ṭakkirāja, who is deep black in color and holds a vajra-hook; in the southwest, Nīladaṇḍa, who is deep black and holds a blue staff; and in the northwest, Mahābala, who is deep black and holds a trident. Acala and the others are all crowned with Akṣobhya. Above, one should contemplate Uṣṇīṣacakravartin, the Lord of Vairocana, who is yellow and holds a yellow wheel. Below, one should contemplate Sumbharāja, who is smoke-colored, crowned with Citteśa (Amitābha), holds a mace, and is terrifying. These wrathful deities (krodhas) have three eyes, hair that stands upright and is tawny, and are adorned with various *nāgas*. They have two arms and one face, are dwarfish with protruding bellies, and should be meditated upon as holding a vajra-noose attached to the raised index finger in their left hands. However, Ṭakki and Acala are graceful, adorned with divine ornaments, and have distorted faces. Furthermore, they should all be seen standing in the *pratyālīḍha* posture upon sun-mandalas on universal lotuses.

In this way, the ten wrathful kings, having established emanations identical to themselves in the form of Yamāntaka and the other wrathful deities in their respective places, join their palms in the *saṃpuṭa* gesture. Facing [the practitioner], the mantra-reciter should visualize them saying: "O wrathful ones, what shall we do? preceded by a praise with the eight-line heart-mantra and the subsidiary-heart mantra. Then, according to the distinction of the rites such as pacification (*śāntika*) and so forth, he should command them with the mantra taught in the *Ḍākinīvajrapañjara*:
oṃ sumbha nisumbha hūṃ | oṃ gṛhṇa 2 hūṃ | oṃ gṛhṇāpaya 2 ānaya hoḥ | bhagavan vidyārāja pūṃ phaṭ ||

With this, the command is given. Then, having received the command of Vajradhara, one goes there oneself and binds the hosts of obstructors such as Indra by the throat with a vajra-noose. Terrifying them with their respective weapons, one consigns them to emanations in the ten directions and should visualize that they remain facing Vajradhara. In this regard, the host of obstructors is as follows: Indra is fair-complexioned, mounted upon the white elephant Airāvata, thousand-eyed, wearing a jewel-crown, and of graceful form. Yama is black, mounted upon a buffalo, with hair standing upright and tawny, dwarf-like, and pot-bellied. Varuṇa is white, mounted upon a celestial tortoise, his head marked by hoods, and of graceful form. Kubera is yellow, riding a man, wearing a jewel-crown, and of graceful form. Īśāna is white, mounted upon a bull, with a crown of matted locks, dwarf-like, and large-bellied. Agni is seated on a goat, his head marked by a crown of matted locks, dwarf-bodied, and red. Rākṣasa is smoke-colored, seated upon a corpse, with disheveled hair, and dwarf-like. Vāta is dark-blue, seated upon a yellow deer, wearing a jewel-crown, and of graceful form. Above is Pitāmaha (Brahmā), yellow, with a swan as his vehicle, dwarf-like, pot-bellied, and wearing a crown of matted locks. Below—

The Earth Goddess, yellow in color, seated upon a lotus, wearing a jewel crown, and possessing a graceful, slender form—these obstacles should be visualized as seized by Vamāntaka and the other deities, terrified and agitated, intent on seeking protection.

Thereafter, having emanated from the seed-syllable in one’s own heart a mass of ten wrathful deities—shaped like spikes below, black in color, most terrible, and as unbearable as the fire of universal destruction; and shaped like the nectar-circling serpent (*amṛtakuṇḍalī*) above—and having projected them onto the heads of the hosts of obstructors, and having commanded the wrathful ones, one should perform the ritual of staking (*kīlayet*).

Oṃ gha gha ghātaya 2 sarvaduṣṭān phaṭ 2! Kīlaya 2 sarvapāpān phaṭ 2! Hūṃ hūṃ! O Vajrakīla, Vajradhara commands: nail down the vajra-body, speech, and mind of all wicked obstructors! Hūṃ 2 phaṭ 2! Thus is the ritual of driving in the stakes. Thereafter, all the wrathful deities strike those stakes with vajra-hammers transformed from their own emblems, until they reach the surface of the earth. With this mantra: Oṃ vajramudgara, strike the vajra-stakes! Hūṃ phaṭ!

Thus is the striking. Then, at the time of unifying with their respective emanations, one should visualize the retinues of obstructors as burnt and utterly eradicated by the blazing fire of wrath. Having thus struck them down and eradicated them, and having become free from obstacles, one subsequently visualizes the sun in front by means of the syllable *repha*, and upon that sun, a crossed-vajra (*viśvavajra*) born from the syllable *hūṃ*.
With that very same vajra, one should visualize a rampart and a cage-like enclosure.

Here, by the word "and" (ca), one should contemplate the net of vajra-arrows, the vajra-canopy, and the ground made of vajras, extending down to the subterranean realm (rasātala), as established [by the text]. Thus ends the protection wheel. 6.
7. Adhimokṣa of Emptiness:
Then, having visualized emptiness as a great protection according to the sequence to be described—since the entire world is indeed visualized by the mind, yet that [mind] is not visualized.
The thorough knowledge of all phenomena is cultivation, yet it is not cultivation at all.
Thereafter, one should recite the mantra that summarizes the essence of the reality of all phenomena without exception: *oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham* ||7||
8. The charnel ground.

In the center of that, one should visualize white wisdom (*prajñā*) in the form of the syllable *E*, pervading space. Above that is a double lotus born from the syllable *Paṃ*. Above that is a double vajra born from the syllable *Hūṃ*. In the center of the altar-platform formed by the double vajra is the wind mandala, blue in color and shaped like a half-moon, born from the syllable *Yaṃ*. Above that is the triangular fire mandala, red in color, born from the syllable *Raṃ*. Above that is the circular water mandala, white in color, born from the syllable *Vaṃ*. Above that is the square earth mandala, yellow in color, born from the syllable *Laṃ*. At the corners are four yellow vajras. Having recognized the consciousness residing in the center of that, one should contemplate all of this transforming into the palace (*kūṭāgāra*), adorned with the eight cremation grounds, appearing instantaneously (*jhaṭiti*).
The eight cremation grounds, endowed with trees and so forth in their respective order, are now described.

To the east is the great cremation ground named Caṇḍogra. There, the tree is the Śirīṣa; the Yakṣa is Gajānana, white in color; the Lord of the Direction is Śakra; the Nāga is Vāsuki, yellow; the cloud is named Garjita, possessing all colors; the mountain is Sumeru, composed of the four jewels; and there stands the Caitya named Sitavajra. (1)

In the south is the great cremation ground named Karaṅkabhīṣaṇa. There is a mango tree; the yakṣa is buffalo-faced and black; the guardian of the direction is Yama; the nāga is Padma and white; the cloud is Āvartaka and multicolored; the mountain is Malaya and fair-complexioned; and there stands a shrine called Kṛṣṇavajra. (2)

In the west is the great cremation ground named Jvālākula. There, the tree is the Aśoka; the yakṣa is Makarānana; the guardian of the direction is Varuṇa, white in color; the nāga is Karkoṭaka, red in color; the cloud is named Ghora, possessing all colors; the mountain is Kailāsa, white; and the caitya stands there, known as Sitasaṃjñāvajra. ||3||

To the north is the great cremation ground named Gahvara. There is an *aśvattha* tree; a yakṣa with a human face and fair complexion; Kubera as the lord of the direction; the black nāga Takṣaka; a cloud of all colors named Ghūrṇita; and the dark mountain Mandara. A shrine named Gaurasaṃskāravajra stands there. (4)

In the northeast is the great cremation ground named Lakṣmīvana. There is a banyan tree; the yakṣa is Gomukha, white in color; the lord of the direction is Maheśvara; the nāga is named Śaṅkhapāla, yellow in color; the cloud is named Caṇḍa, possessing all colors; the mountain is Mahendra, black; and there stands a white caitya named Cittavajra. ||5||

In the southeast is the great cremation ground named Aṭṭaṭṭahāsa. There, the tree is the Karañjaka; the yakṣa is Agānana, who is red; the lord of the direction is Hutāśana; the nāga is Mahāpadma, who is dark green; the cloud is named Ghana, who is multicolored; the mountain is Gandhamādana, who is yellow; and the shrine is red, where the one named Kāyavajra resides. (6)

In the southwest is the great charnel ground named Ghorāndhakāra (Dreadful Darkness). There, the tree is a *latāparkaṭi*; the yakṣa is Kṛṣṇa Mṛtakānana; the guardian of the direction is a rākṣasa; the nāga is Ananta, who is white; the cloud is named Pūraṇa and is multicolored; the mountain is named Hema and is white; and there stands a black *caitya* named Ratnavajra. (7)

In the northwest is the great cremation ground named Kilikilārava. There, the tree is Arjuna; the yakṣa is named Śyāma Mṛgānana; the guardian of the direction is Maruta, who is dark blue; the nāga is Kulika, who is variegated; the cloud is named Varṣaṇa, who is multicolored; the mountain is Nīla, known as Śrīparvata; and the shrine (caitya) stands there, dark blue, named Dharmavajra. ||8||

These yakṣas of great supernatural power (maharddhika) are two-armed; their bodies emerge from the middle of trees. Their left hands, which are lotuses, are occupied with skull-cups (naraka-pāla) filled with blood. Their right lotus-hands are depicted in the gesture of grasping various flavors (rasa). They should be visualized thus. These [forests] are dense with various trees adorned with green meadows, fresh sprouts, leaves, flowers, and so forth. They are graced by flocks of various birds such as crows, cuckoos, owls, parrots, mynas, pigeons, female doves, and vultures. They are filled with various wild animals such as lions, wolves, tigers, leopards, boars, and others. They are crowded with various fragrant flowers. They are terrifying due to being swarming with various serpents. Various regions and places are decorated with bones, skulls, wings, skeletons, skull-bowls, corpses, and so on. Furthermore, various...

The regions were adorned with monasteries, hermitages, meditation halls, groves, and ponds; they were filled with throngs of male and female practitioners of yoga, avadhūtas and avadhūtīs, meditators and meditators, yakṣas and yakṣiṇīs, pretas and pretīs, rākṣasas and rākṣasīs, kumbhāṇḍas and kumbhāṇḍīs, bhūtas and bhūtīs, ḍākas and ḍākinīs, vīras and vīriṇīs, whose minds were intent on the conventions of the *saṃketa*; and they were completely filled by hosts of ḍākas and ḍākinīs who had attained the bliss of laughter, dance, dalliance, embracing, scratching with the nails, and so forth.

Thereafter, some were seen dancing with vajra steps with joyful hearts; some singing with vajra songs; some performing various *samaya* conducts; some consuming the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and the five lamps (*pañcapradīpa*); some offering various articles; some satisfying various sentient beings; and some drinking intoxicants. Others were playing various musical instruments, such as the *ḍāka*, *ḍamaru*, *paṭaha*, *mardala*, *jhara*, lute (*vīṇā*), flute (*veṇu*), and bamboo pipes. Furthermore, they were crowded with hosts of many accomplished ones (*siddhas*), vidyādharas, kinnaras, mahoragas, gandharvas, devas, asuras, and garuḍas, together with their consorts (*prajñā*). There were terrifying, deep abysses filled with shouts of "ki-li-ki-li," yet they were heart-gladdening through the nine dramatic sentiments (*nāṭyarasa*). Together with hosts of *vetāḍas* and spirits (*bhūtas*), these eight cremation grounds (*śmaśāna*) are the purification of the eight consciousnesses (*vijñāna*). Namely: eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), afflicted mental consciousness (*kliṣṭamanovijñāna*), and the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). Thus ends the [description of] the cremation grounds. 8.
9. Gabled chamber (kūṭāgāra)

In its center is a peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*) formed from the transformation of the four great elements—earth, water, fire, and wind—as previously described. Its square vajra-thread is the purification of the five sense faculties; its four gates are the purification of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*); its four archways (*toraṇa*) are the purification of the four right efforts (*prahāṇa*); its four railings (*vedikā*) are the purification of the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*). The four corners, along with the necklaces (*hāra*) and half-necklaces (*ardhahāra*), are the purification of the five powers (*bala*). The eight pillars are fashioned as the purification of the noble eightfold path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*). The decorative friezes (*pakṣiṇī*), cornices (*kramaśīrṣa*), parasols (*cchatra*), yak-tail whisks (*cāmara*), canopies (*vitāna*), bells (*ghaṇṭā*), and banners (*patākā*) are the purification of the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*). Thus, [the entire structure] is the purification of the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*). Such is this dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpanna*), the condensed form of the perfectly pure Buddha-field, the great city of liberation, purified by Vairocana, whose intrinsic nature is luminosity (*prabhāsvara*). One should visualize the peaked pavilion atop a railing of a double-pronged universal vajra (*viśvavajra*). Therein, one should meditate upon the railing: three prongs in the east are white, the southern is yellow, the western is red, the northern is dark green, and the central one is blue.

Now, the arrangement of the sixteen goddesses is described. The five lines [forming the grid] are the Vajra-thread itself. Outside of these, on the panel for the deities, starting from the main entrance and proceeding clockwise with two on each side, there are the worship-deities—the Yoginīs—produced from their respective seed-syllables (bījas) consisting of their own letters joined with a crescent moon and a bindu situated between the moon and sun. They stand in gestures corresponding to their own names: Vīṇā is yellow; Vaṃśā is red; Mṛdaṅgā is smoky-grey; Murajā...

Sita is white; Mālā is yellow; Lāsya is red; Gītā is orange; Nṛtyā is multicolored; Puṣpā is white; Dhūpā is black; Dīpā has a golden luster; Gandhā is yellow; Ādarśā is white; Rasā is red; Sparśā is green; Dharmā is white. All of these should be visualized as seated upon moon-discs, representing the purification of the sixteen digits [of the moon]. The peaked pavilion is adorned by these. (9)
10. The Circle of Causes (*hetumaṇḍala*)

Thereafter, one should visualize within the peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*), upon the pericarp of a multi-colored lotus (*viśvadalakamala*), the four Māras lying supine with their heads pointing north and south: namely, Skandha-Māra, Kleśa-Māra, Mṛtyu-Māra, and Devaputra-Māra. Among these, Skandha-Māra is Brahmā; Kleśa-Māra is Viṣṇu; Mṛtyu-Māra is Maheśvara; and Devaputra-Māra is Indra. These four Māras have their hearts stepped upon by the sun. On the petals in the cardinal directions—east and so forth—are Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara. On the petals in the intermediate directions—northeast and so forth—are Yama, Kubera, Nairṛti, and Vemacitrin. These eight have their hearts stepped upon by the moon. At the very moment of the completion [of the visualization], the peaked pavilion, from the multi-colored lotus up to Vemacitrin, is fully realized.

Above the sun at the heart, through the transformation of the thirty-two vowels beginning with *ā* doubled [to sixty-four], one should visualize a moon mandala indicating the thirty-two major marks (*lakṣaṇa*), which has the nature of the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*). Above that, the thirty-four consonants beginning with *ka*, doubled by means of the six syllables *ḍa, ḍha, ḍa, dha, ya, la* in both direct and reverse order, become eighty syllables; through their transformation, one should perceive a sun mandala indicating the eighty minor marks (*anuvyañjana*), which has the nature of the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*). Within the union [of the two mandalas] is a skull-cup and a flaying knife transformed from the two seed-syllables *hūṃ* and *aṃ*, marked by those very two—this is the wisdom of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*). Then, by the nets of light rays emanating from the two seed-syllables, one should pervade infinite world-systems...

And having brought [the deities] worthy of praise into that very place, one attains the knowledge for performing the rites known as "the unity of all. Through the transformation into unity, one’s own self instantly becomes the form of Śrī Heruka—one’s chosen deity—perfected with sixteen arms, six arms, four arms, or two arms, in the form of the Holder of the Causal Vajra. Likewise perfected, with the neck embraced by Nairātmyā and others, this is the perfectly pure *dharmadhātu-jñāna*. This is the awakening through the five aspects (*pañcākārābhisambodhi*).

In the sequence of the directions starting from the east, one should likewise visualize the eight seed-syllables—*gaṃ caṃ vaṃ ghaṃ puṃ śaṃ caṃ ḍaṃ*—within the *saṃpuṭa* (enclosure) of the moon and sun. One should contemplate the emblems of Gaurī and the others as having evolved from those [syllables]: the curved knife (*kartī*), the skull-bowl (*kṛpīṭa*), the tortoise (*kūrma*), the serpent (*sarpa*), the lion (*siṃha*), the mendicant’s staff (*bhikṣu*), the wheel (*cakra*), and the vajra; these should be visualized as being presided over by those very seed-syllables. Having transformed all this, Gaurī and the others are to be brought forth through the fivefold awakening (*pañcākārābhisambodhi*) according to their colors, emblems, and so forth, in the manner that will be described below. Thus ends the causal maṇḍala. 10.
11. Melting:

Having thus brought forth the form of one’s chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), one should visualize the circle of Ḍākinīs, such as Nairātmyā and the others, together with one’s own consort (*vidyā*), having attained a single flavor (*ekarasa*). Having summoned [the beings] by means of the rays of light from the *samādhi-samaya*, one causes the Gandharva-being, encircled by two rows of red *hoḥ* syllables and consisting of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), to enter through the door of the Ḍāka-wheel. The Blessed One, through the essence of the ultimate supreme great bliss and out of passion for his consort, melts completely and comes to abide in the form of a seed-syllable (*bīja*). Thus is the melting (*drutāpatti*). 11.

12. Then the four goddesses, Pukkasī and the others, being extremely despondent upon seeing the absence of the Lord of the Wheel, and thinking, "We are now without a protector," overcome by great sorrow and longing intensely, they rouse the Blessed One with vajra-songs that awaken the mind.
Arise, O compassionate one! Cry out for me and protect me!
O Great Union of Bliss, fulfill my desire; increase my meditative absorption in the Void.
If you are disturbed, I shall die; arise, O Hevajra!
Enter the state of emptiness, O Śabarī, and let the task be accomplished.
"O Lord of the Suras, having invited the world, why do you depart while it is empty?
I am a Caṇḍālī; I entreat you, for without you I cannot endure."
O Indīālī, arise; I know your heart. We are but low-born Dombī women; do not, do not let your compassionate mind be distracted by us.
Impelled by the song of reality, the Blessed One, through the power of the momentum of his long-standing aspiration, remains as if awakened from sleep.

Yoga is indeed meditative absorption (*samādhi*); therein, this sequence of arising proceeds through five modes of application: consciousness resembling an illusion, like the moon [reflected] in the liquid nectar. Through the transformation of that liquid nectar, there is the *bodhicitta* consisting of the five gnoses. Among these, the moon is the mirror-like gnosis (*ādarśajñāna*), transformed from the syllable *a*; it is that which is transformed from the syllable *ka*.

The mother’s gnosis is the sun. The seed-syllable situated between them, and the symbol produced from the transformation of that seed-syllable, marked by those two, is called "discerning awareness" (*pratyavekṣaṇa*). "All [deities] perform a single activity" refers to "accomplishing activity" (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna*). The completion of the image is the pure *dharmatā*. Then, having brought the moving and non-moving world and the deities of the maṇḍala together through the rays arising from the *bodhicitta* consisting of the five gnoses, and having made them of one flavor right there, one should behold the *bodhicitta* in the form of an autumn moon disc; this is the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) called "yoga."
The so-called "subsequent application" (*anuyoga*) is the meditative absorption (*samādhi*).

Immediately following that, one should behold the spontaneously arisen image (*sahaja-bimba*) transformed from that [absorption], having the form of the autumnal moon, pervading infinite world-systems, with both hands joined in the *dharmamudrā*, consisting of the five gnoses, illusory-like, and the Sahaja-Heruka—this is the meditative absorption called subsequent application. ||12||
13. Nyāsa is atiyoga.

Having thus established the seat of the *bimba*, one should perform the placement of the seed-syllables (*bījanyāsa*) for the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases (*skandhadhātvāyatana*), beginning with Vajrā and ending with Khecarī. One should place *Āṃ* upon the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) for Vajrā; *Iṃ* upon the aggregate of sensation (*vedanāskandha*) for Gaurī; *Īṃ* upon the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñāskandha*) for Vāriyoginī; *Uṃ* upon the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) for Vajraḍākinī; and *Aṃ* upon the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) for Nairātmyā. *Ūṃ* is placed upon the flesh for Pukkasī; *Ṛṃ* upon the blood for Śabarī; *Ṝṃ* upon the seminal essence (*bodhicitta*) for Caṇḍālī; and *Ḷṃ* one should place upon the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*) for Aparagaurī; *Eṃ* upon sound (*śabda*) for Caurī; *Aiṃ* upon odor (*gandha*) for Vettālī; and *Oṃ*...
In the sense-field of taste are the Ghasmaryas; in the sense-field of touch are the Bhūcaryas; in the sphere of phenomena (dharmadhātu) are the Khecaryas. This is the Atiyoga.
The concentration called "not-yoga" is samādhi.

Then, one should place a sixty-four-petaled lotus at the navel, an eight-petaled lotus at the heart, a sixteen-petaled lotus at the throat, and a thirty-two-petaled lotus at the forehead. Having placed the syllables *aṃ*, *hūṃ*, *oṃ*, and *haṃ*, one should contemplate the blessing (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of body, speech, and mind. Having meditated on a white *oṃ* at the head, one should fill the sky with a multitude of *kāyavajra*s from that [syllable] and cause them to enter into that very seed-syllable; thus one becomes the *kāyavajra*. Reciting: *Oṃ, all phenomena have the nature of the *kāyavajra*; I am the nature of the *kāyavajra*.* Having meditated on a red *āḥ* at the path of speech, one should fill the sky with a multitude of *vāgvajra*s from that [syllable] and cause them to enter into that very seed-syllable; thus one becomes the *vāgvajra*. Reciting: *Oṃ, all phenomena have the nature of the *vāgvajra*; I am the nature of the *vāgvajra*.* Having meditated on a black *hūṃ* at the heart, one should fill the sky with a multitude of *cittavajra*s from that [syllable] and cause them to enter into that very seed-syllable; thus one becomes the *cittavajra*. Reciting: *Oṃ, all phenomena have the nature of the *cittavajra*; I am the nature of the *cittavajra*.* The ritual placement (*nyāsa*) concludes with the blessing of body, speech, and mind. This is the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) called "Great Yoga. (13)

14. Then, one whose nature is hatred should, according to the previously mentioned sequence, visualize oneself as the chosen deity among the four forms of Heruka, arisen from the reflection of *sattva*, in union with Prajñā, black in color, and most terrible. One should perceive this being, whose nature is hatred, produced from the moon, seed-syllables, and so forth, within the heart of a sentient being. Having meditated on the hand symbols and other features according to the sequence to be described, one should commence the three pledges (*trisamaya*). Therein, the pledge of self (*ātmasamaya*) is the form of Vajradhara. Within the sun at one’s own heart is the pledge of gnosis (*jñānasamaya*), corresponding to the pledge of self. Within that [sun], one should contemplate the syllable *HŪṂ*, which is the pledge of meditative absorption (*samādhisamaya*).
Thus is the nature of hatred. ||14||
15. The Emission: The Accomplishment of the Mudrā.
Having thus become one whose nature consists of the three samayas, one should begin the accomplishment of the mudrā.
Having attained unwavering wisdom that is affectionate toward practitioners—
wisdom endowed with all auspicious marks and desiring the welfare of all sentient beings.

One should place the syllable Oṃ on her head, the syllable Hūṃ at her heart, the syllable Svā at her navel, the syllable Āḥ on the pair of her thighs, and the syllable Hā on her two feet. As for the placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa), it is performed upon the Goddess just as it is upon oneself.
Vajrā resides in the aggregate of form; Gaurī is remembered in sensation;
Vāriyoginī is in perception; Vajraḍākinī is in mental formations;
and Nairātmyayoginī abides in the nature of the aggregate of consciousness.
Earth is known as Pukkasī, the water element is remembered as Śabarī;
fire should be understood as Caṇḍālinī, and wind is proclaimed as Ḍombī.
Gaurī is always renowned in form; Caurī is proclaimed in sound; Vettālī is in the portion of smell; Ghasmarī is proclaimed in taste;
Bhūcarī is known in touch; and Khecarī arises from the element of phenomena (dharmadhātu).
This is the samādhi called Ādiyoga.

Having thus performed the placement of the seed-syllables within the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases of the Bhagavatī, one should perform the consecration of the lotus and the vajra. Having meditated on a three-petaled lotus that brings delight by means of the syllable *ĀḤ*, and having contemplated the hollow interior of the lotus bud and its filaments by means of the syllable *HŪṂ*, one should then visualize a vajra produced from the syllable *HŪṂ*. Having meditated on the hollow of its jewel by means of the syllable *OṂ*, one should consecrate it with this mantra.
Oṃ! O Lotus, support of bliss, great passion, giver of happiness!
You who partake in the four joys, O Viśva, hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ! Accomplish my purpose!
Oṃ! O Lotus, support of bliss, great passion, giver of happiness!
O you who partake in the four joys, O Viśva! Hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ! Perform my task!
Oṃ! O Vajra of great hatred, bestower of the four joys, Lord whose singular essence is the face of the sky-goer, hūṃ 3! Accomplish my purpose!

In the absence of an external mudrā, having obtained a mentally emanated mudrā and performed the sequence of the assembly of the five families (*pañcakulakalāpa*) and so forth within her, one should begin the act of passion:
*oṃ sarvatathāgatānurāgaṇavajrātmakāḥ sarvadharmāḥ | oṃ sarvatathāgatānurāgaṇavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham*.

Having done this, while uttering the syllable *hūṃ* with the ego-identification (*ahaṃkāra*) of Vāgvajra, one should move the vajra. This is the samādhi called Ādiyoga, beginning with the meditative liberation (*adhimokṣa*) on emptiness and ending with the bliss of delight (*ratisukha*). || ||
Having ascertained that this bodhicitta, which arises from the great bliss of the single flavor of wisdom and means, has emerged from the syllable *phaṭ*, one should perform the offering with this:
*oṃ sarvatathāgatapūjāvajrasvabhāvātmakāḥ sarvadharmāḥ; oṃ sarvatathāgatapūjāvajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham*.

Having recited this, the yogin, assuming the Garuḍa-mudrā, takes that *bodhicitta* situated within the lotus-calyx with the organ of taste and worships himself as being of the nature of all the Tathāgatas and Vajrayoginī. If the mudrā is well-trained, it should be performed; if not, it must not be done, otherwise a root downfall (*mūlāpatti*) will occur. Thereafter, having visualized whatever *bodhicitta* remains as even a tiny drop or particle as transformed into the Lord of the Mandala together with his retinue, one should emit [the offering] through the yoga of the churning-stick and the churner with this: OṂ VAJRADHṚK HŪṂ | BHAGAVATĪ AṂ | GAURĪ GAṂ | CAURĪ CAṂ | VETĀLĪ VAṂ | GHASMARĪ GHAṂ | PUKKASĪ PUṂ | ŚABARĪ ŚAṂ | CAṆḌĀLĪ CAṂ | ḌOMBĪ ḌAṂ ||

Having thus released [the deities] with this mantra, and having caused the welfare of the world to be accomplished, one brings the Blessed One back in. Having caused him to enter by way of the wheel of the Bhagavān-Ḍākinī, the Blessed One remains in the milk just as water is [dissolved] therein, according to the sequence to be described. The Blessed Lady likewise [remains] within the Blessed Lady, and Gaurī and the others are also to be visualized in their respective seats according to their proper places. Thus ends the section on the ritual release (utsarga). 15.

The Knowledge Wheel has sixteen arms, representing the purification of the sixteen emptinesses. One should know that, in sequence, an elephant, horse, donkey, cow, camel, human, śarabha, and wolf reside in the eight lotus-vessels held in the right hands; likewise, in the eight lotus-vessels held in the left hands, there are in order Earth, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Tejas, Candra, Ārka, Yama, and Dhanada.
Cough, asthma, insanity, consumption, leprosy, and scabies, as well as those characterized by enlargement of the spleen and liver— all these are proclaimed [to be the results of such actions].

Thus, by means of the purification of the eight afflictions (*kleśa*), the elephant and the others are taken; and from earth up to Kubera (*Dhanada*), they are taken by means of the purification of the eight sovereign powers (*aiśvarya*). As it is said: "Sovereignty over the body, sovereignty over speech, sovereignty over the mind, as well as supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), omnipresence, mastery, the will, and the agent—this is the group of eight qualities."

Mastery over the body (*kāyaiśvaryam*) is [the power] to manifest infinite bodies. Mastery over speech (*vāgaiśvaryam*) is the ability to speak all languages. Mastery over mind (*cittaiśvaryam*) is the knowledge of the minds of all sentient beings. Mastery over miraculous powers (*ṛddhyaiśvaryam*) is seeing infinite world-systems through supernatural power. Mastery over omnipresence (*sarvagataiśvaryam*) is having a single form throughout the three worlds. By the word *iccha* (desire), "desire" (*kāma*) is expressed; mastery over desire (*kāmaiśvaryam*) is generating great bliss for sentient beings through desire. Mastery over agency (*kartaiśvaryam*) is being the agent, Vajradhara. Mastery over qualities (*guṇaiśvaryam*) is moving about in the form of a deity. The lotus vessel is the purity of the limb of compassion (*karuṇā*). The arms are the purity of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). By this, the non-duality of emptiness and compassion is established. The black limbs are the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*). The eight faces are the purity of the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*). The first face is black for the sake of accomplishing the activity of aversion (*dveṣa*). The left is red for the sake of accomplishing the activity of subjugation (*vaśya*). The right is white for the sake of accomplishing the activity of pacification (*śāntika*). The upward-facing mouth is terrifying and smoke-colored. The western [face] is for the purification of the arisen afflictions such as aversion. Furthermore, the two left faces are black.

Likewise, the two right faces are black for the purpose of destroying the four Māras. Every face has fangs that are formidable, is furrowed with knitted brows, and is most terrifying, possessing a radiance filled with the flames of the fire of universal destruction due to its wrathful nature. It has three red, round eyes; they are red out of compassion. The state of having three eyes is due to the purity of the three vajras and from the thorough knowledge of the three times. He is endowed with twenty-four eyes. His orange hair is tied up on top with a ribbon because he has burned away all afflictions such as passion. His head is marked with a crossed-vajra (viśvavajra) because he acts for the benefit of the world. Above his forehead, he is adorned with a garland of five dried skulls to demonstrate the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) of the five aggregates.

The wheel, the mace, the necklace, the bracelet, and the girdle—thus endowed with the five mudrās through the purity of the five Tathāgatas. The ashes represent the purity of Vajrasattva. "The six mudrās are thus proclaimed. Nakedness is purified by perfect gnosis (*samyagjñāna*), in order to demonstrate that all phenomena are free from obscuration. The four feet correspond to the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*). He stands upon a solar disc with two feet in the *ardhaparyaṅka* posture, performing the dance of *tāṇḍava*, because he has attained the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*). He is the single embodiment of the entire triple world.

The joining of the big toes of the feet is shown for the sake of bestowing [attainments]. Likewise, the wearing of the *alāḍha* foot is for the destruction of obstacles. Hanging from the shoulder is a garland of heads dripping with fresh blood, fashioned from the fifty syllables; through the purification of the fifty syllables of the *āli* and *kāli*, the garland of heads upon the shoulder reveals the path of the unified couple (*yuganaddha*).
It is endowed with the nine dramatic sentiments (rasas): the erotic, the heroic, the loathsome, the furious, the comic, the terrifying, the pathetic, the marvelous, and the tranquil.

Thus it is said. In this context, the aesthetic flavor of *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) consists in being of one taste with Nairātmyā; *vīra* (heroic) in dwelling in the cremation ground; *bībhatsa* (disgusting) in the fierceness of the knitted brows; *raudra* (fierce) in the blazing radiance; *hāsya* (comic) in the wide-open mouth; *bhayānaka* (terrifying) in the garland of moist heads; *karuṇā* (compassionate) in the mind intent on favoring sentient beings; *adbhuta* (wondrous) in the form of Maya; and *śānta* (tranquil) in the state where afflictions such as passion have been abandoned. He should visualize himself as the Blessed One endowed with these qualities. Just as the Blessed One is, so too is the Blessed Lady. Furthermore, she is endowed with the five mudrās, her body adorned with a garland of dried human heads, her left hand holding a skull-cup filled with the blood of gods and asuras, and her right hand holding a flaying knife for the severing of all afflictions. She has a single face to signify that the three realms are of one essence, and she tastes the nectar of the Blessed One’s lips. She is facing [the practitioner].
One should contemplate her as having entered into union with the Blessed One through the savoring of the essence of supreme great bliss by means of the "licked" posture.

One should visualize Hevajra with six arms, representing the purity of the six perfections, and three faces. The central face is black, the right is white, and the left is red. With the two left hands, he holds a trident and a vajra-bell; with the two right hands, he holds a vajra and a flaying knife (*kartī*). With the remaining two hands, joined with a flaying knife and a skull-cup (*kapāla*), he embraces the Vajra-chain (*vajraśṛṅkhalā*) and stands treading upon a corpse.

Furthermore, one should visualize the four-armed Hevajra as the purification of the four Māras: holding a vajra in the right hand and a skull-cup in the left; with the remaining two arms, he is in union with Vajravārāhī; he has one face and stands trampling upon a corpse.
One should visualize the two-armed Hevajra holding a skull-staff (*khaṭvāṅga*) in his left hand and a blazing vajra in his right, treading upon a corpse; his consort is Vajrā.

As for the six-armed deities and others, the remainder—their colors, ornaments, and forms arising from *hūṃ* and so forth—should be understood as being like those of the sixteen-armed deity. Likewise, the Vajraśṛṅkhalā and others are also like Nairātmyā; they all differ only in name.

Having thus determined the Blessed One in the form of one’s own chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), the sequence of colors, symbols, and so forth for the circle of goddesses previously emitted through the yoga of churning and being churned is now set forth by way of their purification.

There, at the eastern gate, one should visualize Gaurī, born from the syllable *gaṃ*, black in color, for the purpose of awakening those beings who are to be trained; she tramples upon Brahmā, has the nature of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), holds a knife in her right hand to cut away false views, and holds a red lotus in her left hand to destroy the latent tendencies of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra-vāsanā*). At the southern [gate], one should behold Caurī, born from the syllable *caṃ*, red in color, for the purpose of awakening those beings to be trained through passion (*rāga*); she holds a sacrificial ladle (*kṛpīṭa*) in her right hand to demonstrate the nature of wisdom and skillful means (*prajñopāya*), and holds a boar in her left hand for the sake of destroying delusion; she tramples upon Śakra and has the nature of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). At the western [gate], one should contemplate Vettālī, born from the syllable *vaṃ*, golden in color, for the sake of nourishing sentient beings; she holds a tortoise in her right hand to demonstrate the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and holds a lotus vessel in her left hand to demonstrate the nature of compassion (*karuṇā*); she is mounted upon Upendra and has the nature of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). At the northern [gate], one should visualize Ghasmarī, born from the syllable *ghaṃ*, resembling a lapis lazuli gem, for the purpose of accomplishing rites of sorcery (*abhicāra-karma*); she holds a snake in her right hand due to the purification of hatred (*dveṣa*), and holds a yogic bowl (*yogapātrī*) in her left hand for the purpose of awakening to the nature of wisdom and skillful means; she is mounted upon Rudra and has the nature of the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). In the northeast, [one should visualize] Pukkasī, born from the syllable *puṃ*, blue in color, for the purpose of awakening the rite of paralyzing (*jambhana*) and for the purification of pride (*māna*); she holds a lion in her right hand—[the rest of the description follows].

One should visualize [the goddess] standing upon Yama, whose nature is the earth element (*pṛthvīdhātu*), holding a battle-axe in her left hand for the purpose of shattering the army of passions and a staff in her right for the purpose of cutting through all dualistic attachments. In the southeast, one should behold Śabarī, born from the syllable *Śaṃ*, who is white in color, for the purpose of awakening peaceful beings and purifying human pride; she stands upon Kubera, whose nature is the water element (*abdhātu*), holding an alms-bowl in her right hand for the purpose of awakening the five wisdoms beginning with the mirror-like wisdom, and holding a *khiṇkhirikā* (small bell) in her left for the purpose of realizing non-dual knowledge. In the southwest, one should behold Caṇḍālī, born from the syllable *Caṃ*, who is sky-blue in color, for the purpose of awakening stubborn beings and accomplishing the rite of immobilization (*stambhana*); she stands upon a Rākṣasa, whose nature is the fire element (*tejodhātu*), holding a wheel in her right hand for the purpose of cutting through mere partial knowledge, and holding a plow in her left for the purpose of uprooting the very foundation of ignorance. In the northwest, one should contemplate Ḍombinī, born from the syllable *Ḍaṃ*, who is multicolored, for the purpose of establishing the welfare of the world and awakening those of cruel disposition; she stands upon Vemacitrin, whose nature is the air element (*vāyudhātu*), holding a blazing vajra in her right hand for the purpose of establishing indivisible wisdom, and holding a threatening gesture (*tarjanī*) in her left for the purpose of threatening all malevolent ones.

In the case of the *jñānamudrā*, however, one should contemplate Nairātmā as having been emitted and entered into the Lord (*bhaṭṭāraka*). Likewise, due to the absence of a seat, Bhūcarī and Khecarī [are to be understood]. Similarly, the emission and re-entry of the others, such as Aparagaurī and so forth, should also be known. By this, the following is stated: as long as there is the ritual placement on the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*), so long is there extraction (*utkarṣaṇa*).

All these [deities] have three eyes and hair that is tawny and stands upright. Their faces are terrifying with bared fangs; they are naked and adorned with the five mudrās. They stand in the *ardhaparyaṅka* posture, performing the *tāṇḍava* dance. Fierce in appearance, they have the form of sixteen-year-olds, are seated upon lunar discs, are produced from the emission of the *bodhicitta*, and are endowed with the desire of the Blessed One.

Now, the purification of the eight seats of Gaurī and the others is described. These seats, beginning with Brahmā and ending with Vemacitrin, are taught for the purpose of severing extreme attachment to passion, knowledge, hearing, drinking, eating, sleep, reasoning, and faith.

Having thus correctly visualized the Blessed One as described—situated within the mandala circle, surrounded by the assembly of Mothers, and pervading the expanse of the sky with a mass of light rays emanating from his own body—one should perform the summoning of the wisdom-circle (*jñānacakra*). From the sun disk located in a skull-cup arising from the syllable *HŪṂ* at the heart-lotus of oneself (the pledge-being), light rays in the form of hooks from the blue syllable *HŪṂ* illuminate infinite world-systems. Having summoned the wisdom-circle and visualized it before oneself, one should offer the water for welcoming, the water for the feet, and so forth; having fully worshipped and praised it, one should perform the acts of summoning, entering, binding, and pleasing with the mantra: *JAḤ HŪṂ VAṂ HOḤ*.
Then: Oṃ vajragaurī ākarṣaya jaḥ | Oṃ vajracaurī praveśaya hūṃ | Oṃ vajravettālī bandhaya vaṃ | Oṃ vajraghasmarī toṣaya hoḥ |

Having caused the wisdom-wheel (*jñānacakra*) to enter the commitment-wheel (*samayacakra*) in its proper manner—like milk merging into milk—one should stabilize the pride of Śrī Heruka. Although the wisdom-commitment (*jñānasamaya*) is identical to one’s own commitment (*ātmasamaya*), nevertheless, immediately after the entry of the wisdom-wheel, one should visualize within one’s own heart the wisdom-commitment of oneself as the consort, red in color, with two arms and one face. Within that [heart], one should also visualize the Lord of Samādhi. Then, one should likewise perceive the letter *Aṃ* situated upon a moon disc on a flaying knife (*kartikā*) produced from the letter *Aṃ*, which resides in the heart-lotus of the Blessed Lady as her wisdom-commitment. Furthermore, one should perceive the signs produced from their respective seed-syllables within the moon discs of the heart-lotuses of the eight Yoginīs as their wisdom-commitments, each further presided over by its own seed-syllable situated upon a moon disc.
The wheel of gnosis. ||16||
17. Regarding the consecration (*abhiṣeka*):

at the time of unifying the wisdom wheel (*jñānacakra*) and the commitment wheel (*samayacakra*), one should draw forth the five Tathāgatas—who have emerged from rays of light from one’s own body—having assumed the form of Śrī Heruka and consisting of the nature of the maṇḍala, along with Vajrayoginī, the great Bodhisattvas, the wrathful deities, and so forth, by beholding them face-to-face in the sky. Having worshipped and praised them, one should pray for the consecration, saying: "May all the Tathāgatas consecrate me! Then those five Tathāgatas [consecrate] with the Victorious flask (*vijayakalaśa*) and others filled with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), just as all the Tathāgatas were bathed immediately upon their birth.
In that manner, I shall bathe you with pure, divine water.
Reciting "Oṃ āḥ, for the glory of the commitment of the empowerment of all Tathāgatas, hūṃ," they perform the bath. Thus is the empowerment. ||17||
18. Sealing (mudraṇa)

At that time, the Vajrayoginīs utter cries of "Victory! Victory! The Bodhisattvas perceive themselves as being fully satisfied; the Wrathful Deities and others rejoice. From the sky, a rain of various fragrant perfumes and flowers falls, and a rain of saffron, sandalwood, and various jewels descends. With the sound of dance, music, and hymns of praise, a great clamor arises throughout infinite world-systems. When the consecration has been performed, the Blessed One becomes the Lord of Mind (Cittesha) upon the glorious seat; likewise for the Blessed Lady. He should be sealed by Akṣobhya, Vairocana, Ratnasaṃbhava, and Amitābha.

Gaurī and the others; furthermore, by those same Buddhas, Pukkasī and the others [are established]. The sealing of the Khecarīs and Bhūcarīs is performed through delusion (moha) and passion (rāga). Then the offering goddesses, Vīṇā and the rest, worship the Lord with their respective specific offerings. Following that, Locanā and the others praise him with songs of eulogy:
"You are surrounded by a multitude of yoginīs; you have obtained the supreme [attainment] within your own mind.
By your compassionate heart, you have beautified this world of moving and non-moving beings; thus you have awakened it."
Do not act with rashness through false pretenses; let your mind be satisfied in the kingdom of Śrī Heruka.
The Tathāgatas, Bodhisattvas, Vidyādevis, Krodhas, and others, remaining in the sky, speak face-to-face by means of the heart-mantras, near-heart-mantras, garland-mantras, and eight-syllable mantras.
Sealing. ||18||
19. The Taste of Nectar

Then, in the midst of the assembly of Mothers, the Vajrī, joined with the Vidyā, brings forth the food of ambrosia (*amṛtabhojana*). By means of the syllable *yaṃ*, there arises a blue wind-maṇḍala in the shape of a half-moon. Following that, a red triangular fire-maṇḍala born from the syllable *raṃ*. Upon that, arising from the syllable *āḥ*, is a lotus vessel resting upon three severed heads; it is white on the outside and red in the center, and is presided over by the syllable *āḥ*. In its center, by means of the mantra beginning with the syllable *buṃ*, one should bring forth the various kinds of food and drink—the five ambrosias (*pañcāmṛta*) and the five lamps (*pañcapradīpa*)—and it is presided over by the syllable *oṃ*. Above that, by means of the syllable *āḥ*, there is a moon-maṇḍala. Above that, one should visualize a white vajra born from the syllable *hūṃ*.

Thereafter, by means of the heat of the fire impelled by the wind, [the offering substance] becomes like the essence of mercury (*pāradarasa*). Having performed its purification, awakening, and kindling with the syllables *HŪṂ ĀḤ OṂ*, one should please the infinite and boundless Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others with rays from the three principles (*tritattva*). Having gone to the world-systems (*lokadhātu*), one brings back the nectar of gnosis (*jñānāmṛta*), unifies it, stirs it with that very vajra, and makes it of one flavor (*samarasīkṛta*). One should visualize the vajra melting into the nectar; one should see it become exceedingly cool through the union of the vajra and the lotus. This is due to the entry of the Tathāgata’s nectar of gnosis. Having thus accomplished it and empowered it with the three principles, one draws it forth with the ladle (*śruvā*). Drawing it forth with the rays of the tongue-vajra born of *HŪṂ*, one offers that nectar during the time of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) according to the distinctions of the rites of pacification (*śāntika*) and so forth. One should likewise meditate upon the deities of the maṇḍala in that same manner. Thus ends "The Taste of Nectar" (19).
20. The benefit of the world:
the samādhi named Maṇḍalarājāgrī (Supreme King of Mandalas).

Following that, through the emanation of the lords of the mandala and their retinues, and by the manifestation of numerous deities—having gone wherever there are disciples who require training according to whatever form is appropriate for each, and having trained them—the Vajra-holder should withdraw those emanations back into his own respective bodies. This is the benefit of the world. From the initial emission [of light] up to the end of the benefit of the world, this is the samādhi named Maṇḍalarājāgrī.
21. The six-limbed meditative absorption named Karmarājāgra.

Thereafter, one should first meditate through *samādhi* on the Black Lord of Meditative Absorption (*Samādhinātha*), who has emerged from the *hūṃ* syllable situated within the moon and sun inside the heart-lotus of the Knowledge-Commitment (*jñānasamaya*) deity. Having visualized him as transforming into the form of a drop (*bindu*), one should see [the deities] emerging via those rays from the pores of the Blessed One’s skin, pervading the entire mandala and its goddesses. One should see them as intensely black. Thus, in the second [instant] they are red; in the third, yellow; in the fourth, green; in the fifth, blue-colored; and in the sixth, white. This should be understood according to the requirements for rites such as pacification (*śāntika*). This is the six-limbed [meditation]. (21)
22. Luminous clarity (prabhāsvara)

Having thus cultivated the six limbs, one should begin with the Clear Light (*prabhāsvara*). Having emanated the rows of vowels (*āli*) and consonants (*kāli*) through inhalation and exhalation—the *āli* emerging via the path of inhalation and the *kāli* via the path of exhalation—one should purify the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) by means of their rays. Having become one with the moving and the unmoving, one should enter into that very [Clear Light] oneself. Then, having withdrawn Gaurī and the others, as well as Nairātmyā, one should perceive all that—both the state of Vajradhara imagined by oneself and everything else—as the Clear Light in its entirety. The sequence for entering the Clear Light is as follows: knowing that Gaurī and the others have emerged from the Bodhicitta, first Gaurī takes her own object and enters the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) of the Blessed One. Likewise, Caurī, Vettālī, Ghasmarī, and Nairātmyā take their respective objects and enter, as appropriate, into feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). Similarly, Pukkasī and the others enter into the elements (*dhātu*) such as earth and so forth. Having thus caused the external group of Mothers to enter, there is then the sequential entry into the five aggregates situated within: the aggregate of form into feeling; feeling into perception; that [perception] into formations; and formations into consciousness. Nairātmyā is considered to be in that [consciousness]. Khecarī and Bhūcarī, having reached both wings, go to the Clear Light; this is to say, they reach Nirvāṇa, which is the Total Void (*sarvaśūnya*). Thus ends the section on the Clear Light. (22)
23. Emergence from meditative absorption.

Now, the emergence from luminosity (*prabhāsvara*). This supreme yoga of luminosity pertains to emergence; for this very reason, the innate (*sahaja*) wisdom of Heruka arises instantaneously. Having meditated in brief upon the Lord of the Mandala—bearing the thirty-two marks and adorned with the eighty minor characteristics, peaceful, and like an illusion—one should contemplate him through the yoga of the vajra-samādhi of the light of wisdom. Thus, there is the arising of the innate. Subsequently, beginning with the innate and ending with luminosity, it should be as follows: from luminosity back to the innate, and from the innate again, one should meditate by this very sequence until the attainment of enlightenment. This is the emergence. 23.
24. Recitation of the mantra.

Regarding the recitation of the mantra (*mantrajāpa*): first, having generated the Blessed One in a form with sixteen arms and so forth, one should contemplate the circle of *ḍākinīs* as before. Thus, the sequence of meditation has been shown according to the four junctions (*saṃdhyā*): the morning junction, the midday junction, the afternoon junction, and the midnight junction. When the practitioner of mantra (*mantrī*) becomes weary from meditation, he should recite the mantra. In this regard, the procedure is as follows: having meditated upon oneself in the form of Śrī Heruka through the yoga of union (*saṃpuṭayoga*) in the center of the wheel, one should visualize the syllables of the mantra issuing from the mouths of the Lord and the goddesses of the mandala, entering the mouth of the Blessed One, passing through the path of the *avadhūtī*, and entering the lotus via the vajra-path. Then, the mantra-syllables, accompanied by rays of light, return again from the mouth of the Blessed One to one’s own mouth. Reciting in this manner without weariness until [the signs of] proximity and so forth appear, one should perform the recitation according to the application of colors. This is the "swinging recitation" (*dolājāpa*).
The syllables of the mantra, radiant and with heads turned upward, should be meditated upon as seated in the form of a circle within the sun at the heart; this is *piṇḍajāpa*.
It should be understood that all the mantra-syllables of the Lord of the Mandala and those of the deities of the mandala are to be recited with a long vowel sound; this is the *samayajāpa*.
Furthermore, the recitation (*jāpa*) should be performed according to the instructions for the heart-mantra, the near-heart mantra, the garland-mantra, and so forth:
*Oṃ deva picuvajra hūṃ 3 phaṭ svāhā*. This is for the sixteen-armed [deity].
Oṃ kiṭi vajra hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. [This is] for the six-armed one.
Oṃ jvalajvalabhyaḥ hūṃ 3 phaṭ svāhā | [This is] for the four-armed one.
Oṃ trailokyākṣepa hūṃ 3 phaṭ svāhā. [This is] for the two-armed [form].
One should recite the heart mantra of all [deities]. Furthermore, the subsidiary heart mantra (*upahṛdaya*) is:
*oṃ vajrakartari hevajrāya hūṃ 3 phaṭ svāhā*.

Oṃ! To the one with eight faces, tawny upright hair and eyebrows, twenty-four eyes, sixteen arms, a body like a black cloud, who wears many garlands of skulls, whose mind is fierce and inflated, and who has fangs like a half-moon: slay, slay, slay! Cause [them] to be done, cause, cause! Roar, roar! Threaten, threaten! Dry up, dry up the seven oceans! Bind, bind the eight nāgas! Seize, seize the enemies! Ha hā hi hī hu hū he hai ho hau haṃ haḥ phaṭ svāhā!
Thus is the root mantra of the Blessed One; likewise is the garland mantra.
Oṃ, to the eight-faced one, hūṃ 2 phaṭ!
Oṃ, to the one whose tawny hair stands upright in whorls, hūṃ 2 phaṭ! Oṃ, to the twenty-four-eyed one, hūṃ 2 phaṭ!
Oṃ, to the sixteen-armed one, hūṃ 2 phaṭ! Oṃ, to the one whose body is like a black cloud, hūṃ 2 phaṭ! Oṃ, to the one who wears many garlands of skulls, hūṃ 2 phaṭ!
Oṃ, to the one with a bloated and cruel mind, hūṃ 2 phaṭ!
Oṃ, to the one with crescent-moon fangs, hūṃ 2 phaṭ!
Thus is the eight-syllable mantra of the Blessed One.
Oṃ aṃ nairātme hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.
Oṃ vajraḍākinīye aṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.
The Heart and Upahr̥daya mantras of the Bhagavatī.
Oṃ aṃ āṃ īṃ uṃ ūṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ ḷṃ ḹṃ eṃ aiṃ oṃ auṃ aṃ phaṭ svāhā.
This is the root mantra of the Bhagavatī.

Oṃ aṃ āṃ hūṃ 2 phaṭ | Oṃ iṃ īṃ hūṃ 2 phaṭ | Oṃ uṃ ūṃ hūṃ 2 phaṭ | Oṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ hūṃ 2 phaṭ | Oṃ lṃ ḷṃ hūṃ 2 phaṭ | Oṃ eṃ aiṃ hūṃ 2 phaṭ | Oṃ oṃ auṃ hūṃ 2 phaṭ | Oṃ aṃ hūṃ 2 phaṭ | This is the eight-syllable mantra of the Bhagavatī. If the recitation of the mantras of Gaurī and the others is performed, then one should perform an embrace of her [the Bhagavatī]. One should also visualize the Bhagavatī upon her seat. In this regard, the mantra is as follows:

Oṃ vajragaurīye hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā | Oṃ vajracaurīye hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā | Oṃ vajravettālīye hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā | Oṃ vajraghasmarīye hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā | Oṃ vajrapukkasīye hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā | Oṃ vajraśabarīye hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā | Oṃ vajracaṇḍālīye hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā | Oṃ vajraḍombinīye hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā ||
The recitation of mantras. ||24||

25. Now the reality of the *bali* offering is explained. Having visualized Sahaja Heruka through the conviction (*adhimokṣa*) in emptiness, one should visualize the Lord of Wrath (*krodheśvara*), the Greatly Terrible One with eight faces and so forth, the Vajra of Hatred (*dveṣavajra*), arisen according to the previously mentioned sequence. Thus, the yogin established in the samādhi of the Vajra of Hatred should emit all ten wrathful deities (*krodha*) born from the syllable *HŪṂ*, surrounded by garlands of flames, and dispatch Yamāntaka and the others to the directions starting with the east. Having summoned the hosts of obstructors such as Indra and the rest, he should command them with the mantra beginning with *Oṃ sumbha niḥsumbha*, etc., according to the specific rites of pacification (*śāntika*) and so forth.

Thereafter, one should visualize the vajra transformed from the elephant-vessel and the vajra-bell transformed from the earth-vessel. In this same manner, it should be applied to the others as well. With the three syllables, one should see three *dharmodayas* situated one above the other, each resting upon a red eight-petaled lotus. [One should visualize] the hosts of obstructors brought by the ten wrathful deities:
Oṃ inda yama jala jakkha bhūta vahni vāyu rakkha canda sujja māda bappa talapātāle aṭṭhasappa svāhā!

Having thus consecrated [the substances], one should perform the summoning and so forth: Oṃ vajragauri ākarṣaya jaḥ | Oṃ vajracauri praveśaya into the three lotuses hūṃ | Oṃ vajravettāli bind them in their respective places vaṃ | Oṃ vajraghasmari subjugate with the bell of power hoḥ |

Having done this, one should visualize [the deities]. Therein, in the central city, on the eastern petal is Indra: holding a vajra in his hand, seated upon a moon, with moon-like radiance, mounted upon the white elephant Airāvata; he has a thousand eyes, two arms, and one face, possesses a graceful body, wears all ornaments, a jeweled crown, and is yellow in color. On the south is Yama: two-armed and one-faced, holding a staff (*daṇḍa*) in his right hand, wearing all ornaments, with brown hair standing upright and blazing, short and pot-bellied, black in color, mounted upon a buffalo, seated upon the sun, and possessing solar radiance. On the west is Varuṇa: white, with a graceful body, one-faced and two-armed, holding a *kumuda* lotus in his right hand, his head marked by a hood, wearing all ornaments, a jeweled crown, mounted upon a crocodile (*makara*), seated upon the moon, and possessing lunar radiance. On the north is Yakṣa: yellow, with a graceful body, one-faced and two-armed, holding a *śrīphala* fruit in his right hand, wearing all ornaments, a jeweled crown, mounted upon a human, seated upon the moon, and possessing lunar radiance. On the northeastern petal is Bhūtapati (Śiva): three-eyed, wearing a crown of matted locks and bearing the moon, his body smeared with ashes, with a graceful body, one-faced and two-armed, holding a trident (*triśūla*) in his right hand, white in color, wearing a tiger-skin garment, adorned with all bone ornaments, having a bull as his vehicle, and seated upon the moon.

[In the center is] Candraprabha. In the southeast petal is Vahni (Fire), red in color, wearing a crown of matted hair, with one face, a short and pot-bellied body, two arms holding a rosary and a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), dressed in red robes, with tawny beard and mustache, mounted upon a goat, seated on the sun, and possessing solar radiance. In the southwest petal is Rākṣasa, black in color, with brownish-yellow hair tied upward, short in stature, with a mouth made terrifying by distorted fangs, one face, two arms, holding a *kaṭṭāraka* (cleaver) and a skull-cup (*kapāla*), wrathful, with furrowed brows, naked, standing upon a corpse, seated on the sun, and possessing solar radiance. In the northwest petal is Vāyu (Wind), dark green, wearing a jewel crown, with one face and a graceful body, two arms both holding a wind-banner (*vātapaṭṭa*), adorned with all ornaments, mounted upon a yellow deer, seated on the moon, and possessing lunar radiance. In the central square is Pṛthvī (Earth), yellow, adorned with all ornaments, with one face and two arms; in her left hand she holds a jar, and in her right she holds a signet of grain resting upon a lotus; she has a graceful body, wears a jewel crown and divine garments, is seated on the moon, and possesses lunar radiance. The *pretas* (hungry ghosts) should be visualized as surrounding the Earth. Indra and the other four [directional guardians] hold a snake-noose in their left hands. All of them, moreover, stand in the *pratyālīḍha* posture—thus one should contemplate.

Upon the eight petals of the lotus situated on the *dharmodayā* above: On the eastern petal is Candra (the Moon), white in color, riding a white horse, wearing a jewel crown, holding a night-lotus (*kumuda*) in his hand, adorned with all ornaments, seated upon a moon-disc, and possessing moon-like radiance. On the southern petal is Sūrya (the Sun), red in color, adorned with all ornaments, wearing a jewel crown, holding a lotus with both hands, riding a green horse, and possessing the radiance of his own breath. On the western petal is Budha (Mercury), fair-complexioned, wearing a jewel crown, holding an arrow in his hand, riding a mouse, seated upon a sun-disc, and possessing sun-like radiance. On the northern petal is Śukra (Venus), blue in color, wearing a jewel crown, holding a spear (*śakti*) in his hand, seated upon a sun-disc, and possessing sun-like radiance. On the petal in the northeast is Maṅgala (Mars), red, with hair tied upward, holding a lotus, seated upon a sun-disc, and possessing sun-like radiance. On the petal in the southeast is Bṛhaspati (Jupiter), yellow, wearing a jewel crown, holding a mace (*gadā*), seated upon a sun-disc, and possessing sun-like radiance. On the petal in the southwest is Śanaiścara (Saturn), black, with tawny hair, holding a trident (*triśūla*), seated upon a sun-disc, and possessing sun-like radiance. On the petal in the northwest are Rāhu and Ketu, dark black and smoky-colored respectively, both seated upon sun-discs and possessing sun-like radiance. Rāhu makes the gesture of devouring as he draws in the wheel of saṃsāra; Ketu has his hands joined in the *saṃpuṭa-añjali* gesture. In the central pericarp is Brahmā, four-faced and four-armed, holding a triple staff (*tridaṇḍa*) and making the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*) with one hand, while the remaining two hands hold a rosary (*akṣasūtra*) and a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*). He is yellow, rides a swan, is stout, wears matted hair and a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), is short and pot-bellied, seated upon a moon-disc, and possesses moon-like radiance. Surrounding Brahmā, one should visualize the Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita, Tuṣita, Yāma, Akaniṣṭha, and other gods, all encircled by their respective deities.

Upon the eight petals of the lotus situated on the *dharmodayā* below, arranged in the sequence of the cardinal and intermediate directions: Vāsuki is yellow; Padma is white; Karkoṭaka is red; Takṣaka is black; on the petal in the northeast (aiśānī) is Śaṅkhapāla, yellow; Mahāpadma is dark blue (śyāma); Ananta is pale white (pāṇḍara); and Kulika is variegated (karbura). These eight have jewel crowns, human bodies and faces, wear all ornaments, and have heads marked by hoods. In the pericarp is the Naga Śeṣa, with a jewel crown, white in color, human-faced, and possessing a hood. Surrounding [the pericarp] are the hosts of asuras and hell-beings to be visualized.

Having thus stabilized these [deities] and having further transformed them, one should manifest them in the form of Śrī Heruka through the application of the seeds of body, speech, and mind. Those situated above, having transformed their own individual forms, arise from the syllable *Oṃ* in the form of Body-Vajra (*kāyavajra*), white in color, and wearing a crown of Vairocana. Those situated below, having transformed their own individual forms, arise from the syllable *Āḥ* in the form of Speech-Vajra (*vāgvajra*), red in color, and wearing a crown of Amitābha. Those situated in the middle, transformed from their respective colors, marks, and postures, arise from the syllable *Hūṃ*; they are black in color, in the form of Mind-Vajra (*cittavajra*), and wear a crown of Akṣobhya. For the sake of all rites, their arms, faces, and so forth should again be made like those of oneself; other ritual acts should be performed according to the appropriate pride (*ahaṅkāra*). For all of them, the form is just as that of oneself.

Having thus reflected, one should offer the guest-water (*argha*) and other honors to the Vajras of Mind, Body, and Speech who have assumed the form of Śrī Heruka. Therein, the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is performed on the head with a bundle of *kuśa* grass;

the water for the feet (*pādya*) is offered at the feet with the *saṃdaṃśa* mudrā; the water for rinsing the mouth (*ācamana*) is offered to the mouth by pouring from a conch held in the left hand with the right hand, using the *śaṅkha* mudrā; and the guest-water (*argha*) is offered three times to the head with the *argha* mudrā. Oṃ, having accepted this supreme honor and sprinkling, svāhā!

Having offered everything with the mantra beginning with "ityādi," and having worshipped with flowers, incense, and so forth; preceded by the root, heart, and near-heart mantras and praises, one should—according to the previous procedure for tasting nectar (*amṛta*)—produce the offering of the *bali* as nectar. Then, preceded by the gestures (*abhinaya*) of the lotus-turning (*kamalāvarta*) and others, and following the embrace, one should perform the binding of the mudrās. Visualizing at the tips of their tongues and on one's own a white five-pronged vajra, the size of a barley grain, produced from the syllable *HŪṂ*, one should, while brandishing the vajra and ringing the bell, consume [the offering] oneself, drawn in through the tube of the tongue which is a ray of light arising from the *HŪṂ*-born vajra. One should feed these [deities]. Thus, one should contemplate: "They are tasting [it] through the tube of the tongue which is the vajra born from *HŪṂ*."
Eat this offering; smell the flowers and incense; consume the meat! Accomplish all our purposes; destroy the thorns of our enemies.
Thus, with the first half of this [verse], one should offer food; and with the second half, the task [to be performed].

Thereafter, the mantra-practitioner, holding the vajra and bell, performs the brandishing of the vajra and the ringing of the bell in the eight auspicious positions preceded by the *kamalāvarta* and other gestures. Reciting "Oṃ, the letter A is the mouth of all phenomena because they are unoriginated from the beginning; Oṃ Āḥ Pūṇ Phaṭ Svāhā," one should perform the act of pleasing with this very [mantra]. And the twilight song should be sung in a high-pitched, faltering tone: "In Kollair there is the cry of 'mummuṇi'; in Kakkola there is the sound of 'kakkolā'.
The cloud is thick and heavy; alas, compassion is not being practiced."
There, meat is eaten greedily and strong liquor is drunk;
O Kāliñjara, there the mouse is sold as merchandise.
Camphor, kastūrī, frankincense, and camphor are brought there;
jasmine flowers serve as fuel, and rice is eaten there.
While spitting at the spectacle, one does not distinguish between the pure and the impure;
though a necklace of pearls is placed upon a limb devoid of light, it is there that the glass trinket is sold.
The Malājas and Kundurus dance, yet the ḍiṇḍima drum is not sounded there.
