Having performed the praise consisting of the root mantra, the eight lines, the heart, and the near-heart, one should recite the hundred-syllable mantra:

Oṃ śrīheruka, preserve the samaya! Abide as Heruka! Be firm for me! Be well-disposed toward me! Be nourishing to me! Be devoted to me! Grant me all accomplishments! And in all activities, make my mind auspicious! Hūṃ ha ha ha ha hoḥ! O Blessed One, Vajra of all Tathāgatas, do not abandon me! Be Heruka! O Great Samayasattva! Āḥ hūṃ phaṭ!
Following that is the empowerment through truth (satyādhiṣṭhāna):
"The goddesses are the authority, the samaya is the authority, and their spoken words are the supreme authority."
By this truth, may these goddesses become the cause of my favor.
One should recite the Anukampā [verse]:
"Those who are indifferent to both worldly existence and its cessation, whose attachment to conceptual constructs has been shattered,
and who perceive all phenomena as being like space from the perspective of ultimate reality."
O Goddesses, whose minds are oceans overflowing with the waters of profound compassion, show me the utmost mercy! Show it, show it!

Thereafter, having honored [the deity] with water for rinsing the mouth, water for wiping the hands, fragrant betel, flowers, and so forth; having made a request for one's desired aim with palms joined in *añjali*; having offered auspicious benedictions for the king and others; having recited the verse beginning with "He who is Dharma..."; and having asked for forgiveness, one should then dismiss [the deity] with: *oṃ vajra muḥ | oṃ āḥ hūṃ phaṭ 3*.
One should perform the dedication with the syllable Oṃ; the gratification with the syllable Āḥ; the satisfaction with the syllable Hūṃ; and the withdrawal with the threefold Phaṭ.
If, by means of this strength, yogins perform worship toward all beings for the sake of auspiciousness,
then there will be untroubled happiness within them.
And the gods are pleased, as are the well-being of the world.
It bestows subjugation, malevolent rites, the destruction of enemy armies, eradication, killing, and summoning;
it shall grant peace, happiness, and nourishment.
Whatever offering is here constantly made to the host of spirits.
The meditative absorption named Karmarājāgra extends from the six limbs and so forth up to the principle of the offering (balitattva).

When one becomes afflicted by wind through the power of [past] mental cultivation, then, first of all, for the sake of its remedy, one should meditate on a lunar disc produced from the syllable Oṃ at the head. One should visualize oneself as being nourished by a great rain of nectar that has entered within the mind, until health is restored. (25)
26. Subtle Yoga:
"Subtle Yoga" is the name of a meditative absorption (*samādhi*).

Then, the practitioner situated in the center of the wheel should visualize four lotuses—at the navel, the heart, the throat, and the forehead—having sixty-four, eight, sixteen, and thirty-two petals respectively. Having visualized this, he should contemplate the seed-syllable at the navel. Blazing like the flame of a lamp in the form of Caṇḍālī, it burns the five Tathāgatas and Locanā and the others residing in the Dharma-wheel; it also burns the Saṃbhoga-wheel, which is accompanied by the inhalation and exhalation of the vowels and consonants (*ālikāli*), as well as the *haṃ* syllable in the form of consciousness located in the Mahāsukha-wheel. Then, taking up the bodhicitta which is the cause of great bliss, and having made it of one flavor with Suchness together with the Blessed One, he again takes hold of the moon, the sun, and the skull-cup, and causes them to enter the seed-syllable at the heart. That seed-syllable becomes intensely radiant, accompanied by resonance (*nāda*), and consists of the nature of the five Tathāgatas. Again, emerging from that resonance like the flame of a lamp, it [becomes] the letter *ū*, the form of envy (*īrṣyā*). The letter *rā*—

The letter *ga* into the letter *ha*; the letter *ha* into the line whose nature is slander (*piśuna*); the line into the half-moon whose nature is delusion (*moha*); the half-moon into the drop (*bindu*) whose nature is hatred (*dveṣa*); the drop into the resonance (*nāda*); and one should contemplate even the resonance as the subtle pinnacle (*sūkṣmakoṭi*). By means of that, through the state of oneness, there will undoubtedly arise the stabilization of the mind. Through the mere stabilization of the mind, effortlessly, one should cause to radiate the array of the Tathāgatas, the net of Yoginīs, and the mandala-circle in its full extent, pervading infinite world-realms. This is the meditative absorption named "Subtle Yoga" (*sūkṣmayoga*). ||26||

27. The second placement (*nyāsa*): Having arisen from that, or otherwise, the yogi should wander after performing the two-arm *Hevajra* yoga. One should contemplate the armor (*kavaca*) as follows: Akṣobhya in the form of a crown (*cakrī*), with *hūṃ* at the head; Amitābha in the form of divine earrings, with *hrīḥ* on the ears; Ratneśa in the form of a necklace (*mālā*), with *trāṃ* at the throat; Vairocana in the form of bracelets (*rucaka*), with *oṃ* on the hands; Amoghasiddhi in the form of a girdle (*mekhalā*), with *khaṃ* on the waist; and Vajrasattva in the form of ashes, with *haṃ* on all limbs. Thus one should contemplate the armor.

At the two eyes is Mohavajrī, Āṃ; at the two ears is Dveṣavajrikā, Aṃ; at the nose she is known as Mātsaryakī, Iṃ; at the mouth is Rāgavajrikā, Īṃ; for touch is Īrṣyāvajrī, Uṃ; and at the mind is Nairātmayoginī, Aṃ.
"O Great Being, [wear] this armor for the purification of the sense faculties.
Thus ends the second placement (*nyāsa*). ||27||

28. Having been thus equipped with the armor forged by Vajrayoginī, the Tathāgatas, and others, the yogi should roam like a lion within the palace of the three worlds through the practice of the two-armed Hevajra. As it has been said by the venerable Nāgārjuna:
"This is not a peaked pavilion, nor are these the three worlds, nor are these living beings; they are the Victors."
I am the Lord of the Mandala, not a human being; nor are there sense objects, nor sense faculties, nor the earth and other elements;
nor are there forms and so forth, for they consist of the nature of reality (dharmatā). These are the deities of the mandala.
O mind, as you contemplate the entire universe as the mandala-circle, why do you wander in delusion?
Thus ends the section on wandering. ||28||

Thereafter, whatever food, drink, or other substances have been acquired or obtained by the yogin, having purified them as before and consecrated them with the three-syllable mantra, he should consume them according to the procedure for tasting nectar; this is the meal. (29)
One should avoid greed, delusion, fear, anger, and shameful conduct;
having cast off sleep and the self, the practice is performed— of this there is no doubt.
Having given the gift of the body, one should thereafter undertake the practice;
therefore, no gift is given with a calculation of what is or is not a share.
One should consume whatever food, soft fare, or drink is obtained;
one must not form attachments here through the conceptualization of the desirable and the undesirable.
That which is endowed with five colors is conceived as a single color;
for just as through many [colors] a single color arises, no differentiation occurs.
Meditation is said to be auspicious when practiced under a solitary tree or in a cremation ground,
likewise at night in a mother’s house, or else in a lonely wilderness.
If one desires to engage in the conduct once some degree of "heat" has been attained,
and if one wishes to attain accomplishment, one should practice by means of this very conduct.

Such is the detailed explanation. "Conduct" (*caryā*) means the practice of conduct; that is to say, staying, worldly interaction, or behavior. This was stated with reference to having attained some degree of "heat" (*ūṣmagata*). Furthermore, the beginner yogi should move about discreetly in his own place at night until some slight gain is achieved. Why is this? Because of the statement: "In such a way that no disclosure occurs. Once the gain has been obtained, he may act or not act as he pleases; thus is "conduct" defined. (30)
31. Then, at the subsequent twilight, having brought the yoga of Śrī Heruka to manifestation with the desire to lie down, one should lie down like a lion. Thus is the lying down. 31.

32. Furthermore, regarding "rising again": when it is time to rise and one is exhorted by the songs of the *pukkāsīs* and others, one should perform everything previously described—from the wheel of worship (*pūjācakra*) up to the foot [steps]—at the three junctions of the day, until the form of the maṇḍala circle is directly perceived. Upon the realization of the generation stage (*utpattikrama*), the beginner yogin becomes a lord of the eight stages and travels from buddha-field to buddha-field. And it was said by the Blessed One:
As long as there is the application of cultivation, so long is one a beginner;
through the yoga of a beginner, one may attain the eighth stage.
Furthermore, there is rising again. ||32||
When the steadfast one, having shattered worldly stability, reaches the cessation that is free from conceptual construction,
he may perform all activities; the Buddhas always behold him.
The unsurpassed Five Stages, proclaimed in the glorious *Heruka-tantra-rāja*, elucidated by the venerable Śrī Jālandharipāda, is the profound thought of the Gurus.
Having obtained that which brings fortune to the entire mass of sentient beings, I have composed this excellent merit; by its power, may the world surely attain the supreme form of Hevajra.
The Illumination of the Unsurpassed *Hevajra* in Five Stages is completed. This work is by the feet of the great maṇḍala master, the venerable Rāhulagupta.
Of those phenomena that arise from causes, the Tathāgata has explained their cause, as well as their cessation; such is the teaching of the Great Śramaṇa.

This is the religious gift of the supreme follower of the Mahāyāna, the eminent lay devotee (paramopāsaka) Śrīrāṇa. Whatever merit is herein, may it, preceded by [the dedication for] his preceptors, teachers, mother, and father, be for the attainment of the fruit of unsurpassed knowledge by the entire mass of sentient beings. This was written on the 14th day of Bhādra in the Śaka year 1104, at 2,800 years, 11 months, and 5 days after the final nirvāṇa of the Blessed One, the Lion of the Śākyas, by the novice (śrāmaṇera) Śrījitāriśrī, a resident of the Dharmadhātu Monastery.
